clinicalPearls: Autosomal inherited deficiency of coagulation factor XI, notably common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations but found worldwide.
Bleeding is characteristically injury-related and unpredictable, affecting tissues rich in fibrinolytic activity such as the mouth, nose, urinary tract and after tonsillectomy or dental extraction.
The bleeding phenotype correlates poorly with the plasma factor XI level, so a severely reduced level does not reliably predict serious haemorrhage.
Spontaneous haemarthroses and deep muscle bleeds typical of haemophilia A and B are uncommon.
Screening shows a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time; diagnosis rests on a specific factor XI assay.
Menorrhagia and postpartum haemorrhage are frequent presentations in women.
Antifibrinolytic agents are valuable, particularly for mucosal and dental procedures; factor XI concentrate or plasma is reserved for higher-risk bleeding or surgery.
Some patients develop inhibitory antibodies, especially those with severe deficiency exposed to factor XI-containing products.
reference.pathophysiology: Factor XI is a plasma serine protease zymogen that participates in the intrinsic pathway and, more importantly, in the amplification of thrombin generation. Once the initial tissue-factor-driven burst of thrombin is formed, thrombin activates factor XI on the platelet surface, and activated factor XI in turn activates factor IX, sustaining and consolidating clot formation and stabilising the fibrin plug against premature lysis. Inherited deficiency, caused by mutations in the F11 gene and usually autosomal recessive though heterozygotes may also bleed, reduces this amplification loop. Because the primary haemostatic response and the initiating thrombin burst remain intact, many patients haemostase adequately for most challenges; however, in tissues with high local fibrinolytic activity the impaired thrombin-driven activation of the fibrinolysis inhibitor and the weakened clot leave patients vulnerable to delayed or prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery. This mechanism explains why the bleeding tendency is injury-provoked, variable and only loosely related to the measured factor XI level, and why antifibrinolytic therapy is especially effective at mucosal sites.
additionalDifferentials: Other contact factor deficiencies (factor XII, prekallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen) which prolong the APTT but do not cause bleeding
Acquired coagulopathy from liver disease or vitamin K deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time
Mixing study to distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor
Assays of factors VIII, IX and XII to exclude combined or alternative deficiencies
von Willebrand factor and platelet function testing where mucosal bleeding is prominent
F11 gene analysis in selected cases and for family screening
Inhibitor (Bethesda-type) assay in previously exposed or refractory patients
redFlags: Excessive or delayed bleeding after tonsillectomy, dental extraction or urological surgery
Postpartum haemorrhage or heavy menstrual bleeding causing anaemia
Unexpected surgical bleeding in a patient with an unexplained prolonged APTT
Bleeding failing to respond to replacement, suggesting an inhibitor
Any central nervous system or airway bleeding after trauma
reference.prognosis: With appropriate perioperative and peripartum haemostatic planning most patients have an excellent outlook and a normal lifespan. The unpredictable, largely trauma-related bleeding pattern means the main risks arise around surgery, dental work and childbirth rather than from spontaneous haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Assuming a low factor XI level predicts severe bleeding, or that a mildly reduced level is safe
Confusing factor XI deficiency with harmless contact factor deficiencies that also prolong the APTT but never bleed
Overlooking the strong role of antifibrinolytics and over-relying on factor replacement
Failing to consider an inhibitor when bleeding persists despite replacement
Not screening at-risk family members, particularly in populations with high carrier frequency
references: United Kingdom Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation guidance on rare bleeding disorders (standard reference)
